(a) where-a-boat-carries-its-owner — ANSWERED BY RULING, not by a child voyage. 2026-08-10-the-ticket-owns-the-refusal settled the address from above: the intentions own their tickets, a ticket owns its workflow, and the workflow IS the boat — so the owner is read from the TICKET, which is what `boat_id` has always been. The open question this child carried was real and the ruling dissolved it rather than resolving it: the ticket's `owner` field is indeed the wrong namespace, so the read does not use it. A NEW field, `owning_intention`, carries the address, declared in CairnCommons/tickets/_charter+why.json and distinguished from its two neighbours BY SHAPE — it resolves; they are prose. The child is therefore closed without being built, and closed by an authority above it. No separate ticket was cast for it, because there is nothing left to decide.

THE FALSIFIER ABOVE IS AMBIGUOUS ABOUT THE SIGN OF ITS OWN NON-HOLLOW CHECK, and it is ambiguous about exactly the thing it was written to pin. Its parenthesis — 'the reverted direction is green here, which is the tell' — is true of the TICKET-TIME tooth (a tooth asserting 'this exploit call succeeds' would be green on reverted code) but reads naturally as a claim about the BUILT tooth, which is the opposite. A later reader checking the wrong direction would find the wrong answer and believe it. The original wording stands (it is the evidence that this happens); the unambiguous statement, and the one actually run, is: THE EXPLOIT CALL — an actor with no standing naming ITSELF the owner of a boat it does not own — SUCCEEDS ON REVERTED CODE AND IS REFUSED ON BUILT CODE. Run both directions 2026-08-10. Reverted: the authority rung PASSED the call (it was stopped further along by proven-space, an unrelated gate, which is the rung under test letting it through). Built: Unauthorized, and no record written. The proof file itself does not survive the revert — it imports names the old module does not have — which is a second, cruder witness to the same thing.

THE GRANT ASSUMPTION, named at cast and DISCHARGED by the build. At cast: `Grant.authorizes()` compared `by_owner == owner` where `owner` was the same caller-supplied `boat_owner`, so a caller who could state the owner could mint itself a grant from that fiction and the comparison would hold. Closing only the direct branch would have moved the hole one door along rather than shutting it. `mint_grant` now reads the boat too — it takes `minted_by`, resolves the boat's owner from disk, refuses a minter that owner does not admit, and stamps `by_owner` from the READ value rather than from anything the caller said. Tooth: test_a_grant_minted_from_an_owner_the_minter_invented_authorizes_nothing. A SECOND ASSUMPTION SURFACED DURING THE BUILD AND IS NAMED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT IN THE CHART: the decompose stage predicted that a cleared crossing would honestly record `delegated: true` always. It would not. cairn/tools/base/transitions.py:749 reads that field to render '(delegated)' on the crossing's standing line, so a constant there would mark every crossing delegated and inform nobody. The word keeps the distinction it has always drawn — a per-operation grant was spent — and the rejected reading is recorded inline at the emit call. That is a partial kill of hypothesis 6 and it is dispositioned as one in the verdict.

P1 — P1 and not P0 because the gate it sits in is doing real work today: three of clearance's four refusals — proven-space, resources, legality — read from somewhere the caller does not write, and they are now binding on every crossing into a rest. What is vacuous is the fourth, and the failure it guards against (a device advancing a boat it does not own) has no live instance yet, because the box has one hand. It becomes P0 the day a second mover exists. It is not P2 because harbor_master's charter names this exact failure as its own falsification condition, and a component whose falsifier is met reads green while nothing derives red (Law 9).
